The word nave is a noun with two distinct meanings. Both are correct, but one is far more commonly used today.
Meaning 1: The Central Hall of a Church (Most Common Use)

This is the meaning you will encounter most often in your life.

The nave is the long, central section of a church building — the large main hall where the congregation (the ordinary worshippers) sit during a service.

Picture a traditional Christian church from above. It often looks like a cross. The nave is the longest arm of that cross — the big, open central corridor that stretches from the main entrance door all the way down to the altar area at the far end. When you walk through the front doors of a grand cathedral and see rows of benches (called pews) lined up on either side of a central walkway, with tall pillars and a high ceiling above — everything in that sweeping central space is the nave.

What makes the nave distinct from the rest of the church?

A church is made up of several different zones, and the nave is just one of them. Here is how the nave relates to the others:

  • The nave vs. the aisles. Running alongside the nave — on one or both sides — are narrower parallel corridors called aisles. These are separated from the nave by a row of columns or pillars. The nave is the central and tallest of these parallel sections; the aisles are the lower, narrower ones beside it. So the "nave" is not the entire floor of the church — it is specifically the middle section.
  • The nave vs. the chancel. The nave is the congregation's space — where the people sit. The chancel is the section beyond it, closer to the altar, reserved for the clergy and choir. There is usually a visible dividing point between the two, sometimes marked by a screen, a step, or an archway called the chancel arch.
  • The nave vs. the transepts. In a cross-shaped church, the transepts are the two arms that stick out to the left and right, forming the "arms" of the cross. The nave is the long forward section — the "body" below the arms.
  • The nave vs. the narthex. Some churches have a small entrance hall or lobby right inside the front doors, before you reach the main hall. That entrance lobby is called the narthex. The nave begins after it.

So in the simplest terms: the nave is the main, central, open hall of a church where the ordinary congregation gathers — the dominant interior space that gives the building its sense of grandeur and length.

This word is used in both grand cathedrals and smaller parish churches. Architects, historians, and anyone writing or talking about church buildings use it routinely. You might read: "The restoration team focused on the nave's ceiling," or "The procession walked the length of the nave."
Meaning 2: The Hub of a Wheel (Older, Less Common)

The nave also refers to the hub of a wheel — the thick, solid, cylindrical block at the very center of a wheel, through which the axle passes, and from which the spokes radiate outward.

Think of a traditional wooden wagon wheel or a wooden cart wheel. It has three parts: the outer rim, the spokes that connect the rim to the center, and the solid central block at the heart of the whole structure. That central block is the nave (also called the hub).

This meaning is old and is rarely used in modern everyday speech. You are most likely to encounter it in historical writing, literature from earlier centuries, or technical descriptions of traditional wheel-making. If someone today says "nave," they almost certainly mean the church nave — not the wheel hub.

—Nave (Church)Nave (Wheel)

In a church: The nave is the long, tall, central hall — the congregation's space, running from the entrance to the altar end, flanked by aisles on the sides.

In a wheel: The nave is the central hub — the solid block at the middle of the wheel through which the axle passes.

The church meaning is the one that matters most for modern reading, writing, and conversation. If you remember one thing, remember this: walk into a great cathedral, look down that long, soaring central hall stretching toward the altar — that entire magnificent space is the nave.
